clinicalPearls: Basic calcium phosphate (BCP) crystals, predominantly carbonate-substituted hydroxyapatite, deposit in periarticular soft tissues such as tendons and bursae and also within joints
The commonest clinical expression is calcific periarthritis or tendinitis, classically calcific tendinitis of the rotator cuff at the shoulder

BCP crystals are minute and non-birefringent, so they are not seen on standard polarised microscopy; clumps may stain with alizarin red, but definitive confirmation needs special techniques such as electron microscopy
Acute calcific periarthritis presents with sudden severe periarticular pain, swelling, and tenderness, most often at the shoulder, and can mimic gout, infection, or acute CPP arthritis
Radiographs may show amorphous, cloud-like periarticular calcific deposits that can change or resorb over time, unlike the linear chondrocalcinosis of CPPD
BCP deposition is implicated in severe destructive arthropathies, most notably Milwaukee shoulder syndrome
Treatment is largely symptomatic, using anti-inflammatory therapy, aspiration or needling (barbotage) of deposits, and physiotherapy, as there is no specific crystal-dissolving agent
reference.pathophysiology: Basic calcium phosphate crystals, chiefly hydroxyapatite, form and deposit in periarticular structures and cartilage, often at sites of tissue turnover or degeneration. When crystals are shed into a bursa, tendon sheath, or joint they provoke an acute inflammatory reaction, producing calcific periarthritis. Within joints, BCP crystals can stimulate synovial cells to release proteolytic enzymes that degrade cartilage and periarticular tissue, contributing to rapidly destructive arthropathies. Because the crystals are non-birefringent and extremely small, their detection is far harder than for urate or calcium pyrophosphate crystals.
additionalDifferentials: Rotator cuff tear or subacromial impingement
additionalInvestigations: Radiographs for amorphous periarticular calcification and to track its resorption
Ultrasound for calcific tendinitis or deposits and to guide aspiration
Joint or bursal aspiration with cell count and culture to exclude infection
Polarised microscopy (which will not show the crystals) with alizarin red staining to suggest BCP
MRI where soft-tissue or rotator cuff pathology needs clarification
Electron microscopy in cases of diagnostic uncertainty or for research confirmation
redFlags: Rapidly destructive shoulder or joint pathology suggesting Milwaukee shoulder
Features indicating possible septic arthritis or bursitis
Large deposits causing mechanical symptoms or nerve compression
reference.prognosis: Acute calcific periarthritis is usually self-limiting and the deposits may resorb, with good recovery; however, BCP-associated destructive arthropathies such as Milwaukee shoulder can cause substantial and progressive joint damage.
pitfalls: Missing BCP disease because the crystals are invisible on routine polarised microscopy
Confusing amorphous BCP calcification with the linear chondrocalcinosis of CPPD
Treating self-limiting acute calcific periarthritis as infection unnecessarily
Overlooking an underlying destructive arthropathy driven by the crystals
management: Treat acute calcific periarthritis with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs as first-line anti-inflammatory therapy, with colchicine as an alternative
Aspirate the affected joint or bursa for cell count and culture to exclude septic arthritis before any injection
Give an ultrasound-guided peri-tendinous or intra-articular corticosteroid injection for severe or refractory attacks once infection is excluded
Offer ultrasound-guided needle barbotage (aspiration and lavage) of calcific rotator-cuff deposits in persistent calcific tendinitis
Support recovery with rest, ice and physiotherapy to restore shoulder range of movement
In Milwaukee shoulder, use analgesia, aspiration of large effusions and physiotherapy, reserving shoulder arthroplasty for advanced cuff arthropathy
Refer to rheumatology or orthopaedics for destructive or recurrent disease and image-guided procedures
